article.audioae.title: Audio Autoencoder on Mel Spectrograms
article.audioae.subtitle: Self-supervised audio representation project: signal preprocessing, conversion to log-mel spectrograms, training of a convolutional autoencoder, and approximate audio reconstruction.
article.audioae.overview.title: Overview
article.audioae.overview.text: Objective: learn a compact representation of audio signals without labels by training an autoencoder to reconstruct mel spectrograms. The project demonstrates how to move from a raw waveform to a time-frequency representation suitable for convolutional networks, and how to evaluate reconstruction quality both visually and perceptually.
article.audioae.dataset.title: Dataset
article.audioae.dataset.text: The project uses the TinySOL dataset, which consists of monophonic recordings of isolated instruments. Each sample is resampled to 16 kHz, trimmed or padded to a fixed duration of one second, and amplitude-normalized to produce consistent inputs and facilitate training.
article.audioae.preprocessing.title: Audio Preprocessing
article.audioae.preprocessing.text: Each waveform is converted into a mel spectrogram using an STFT, then compressed on a logarithmic scale. This step produces a more compact and numerically stable representation while emphasizing the frequency structures that are most relevant for learning.
article.audioae.representation.title: Representation: Log-Mel Spectrograms
article.audioae.representation.text: Log-mel spectrograms transform a 1D audio signal into a structured 2D representation that is well suited for convolutional models. Compared to raw waveforms, this representation is easier to model, more interpretable visually, and significantly more efficient for training.
article.audioae.model.title: Model
article.audioae.model.text: The model is a 2D convolutional autoencoder applied to log-mel spectrograms. The encoder consists of convolutional layers followed by normalization and pooling, progressively reducing spatial dimensions while increasing the number of channels. This process extracts increasingly abstract features from the audio signal. The spectrogram is then projected into a low-dimensional latent space using a linear layer, forcing the model to compress the essential information. The decoder performs the inverse operation using transposed convolutions, progressively reconstructing a spectrogram with the same size as the input. Training relies on a reconstruction loss, allowing the model to learn a compact and structured representation of the signal without supervision.
article.audioae.training.title: Training
article.audioae.training.text: Training is performed on the full dataset using a reconstruction loss that combines MSE and L1 to balance optimization stability and detail preservation. The spectrogram dimensions are compatible with the network’s downsampling and upsampling operations, ensuring a consistent reconstruction at the output.
article.audioae.inference.title: Inference and Evaluation
article.audioae.inference.text:
During inference, a validation spectrogram is passed through the autoencoder and compared to its reconstruction.

Evaluation is first performed visually by comparing the global structures of the spectrograms: the main harmonics and the temporal evolution of the signal are generally well preserved, indicating that the model has captured the dominant audio characteristics. However, some differences appear in low-energy regions and fine details, reflecting information loss due to compression in the latent space.

An absolute error map is also computed by taking the point-wise absolute difference between the original and reconstructed spectrograms. This visualization highlights where reconstruction is less accurate: errors tend to be lower in dominant regions of the signal and higher in noisy or low-energy areas.

Finally, an auditory evaluation is performed by reconstructing an approximate waveform using InverseMelScale and Griffin-Lim. The resulting audio remains degraded, mainly due to the absence of phase information in the spectrogram representation.
article.audioae.results.title: Results
article.audioae.results.text: The model successfully reconstructs the overall harmonic structure of the samples, with reconstructed spectrograms that are visually close to the inputs. The reconstructed audio, however, remains more degraded than the spectrogram itself, highlighting the difficulty of converting mel spectrograms back to waveforms and the importance of phase in audio perception.
article.audioae.conclusion.title: Conclusion and Next Steps
article.audioae.conclusion.text:
This project highlights the ability of convolutional autoencoders to learn compact representations of audio signals from spectrograms. The model effectively captures the global structure of the signal, while also illustrating its limitations in preserving fine details and reconstructing audio, particularly due to the absence of phase information.

Several improvements can be explored, such as increasing spectral resolution, using variants like variational autoencoders, or integrating neural vocoders to improve the quality of the reconstructed signal. Further analysis of the latent space could also enable applications such as interpolation or similarity search between audio signals.
